title: JavaScript, from functions to a small project
description: Build a practical foundation in functions and arrays, then write a small order-total calculator. Includes a silent code walkthrough, examples, and a written project submission. Graduation demonstration course.

lessons.title: Functions: inputs, outputs, and useful checks
Arrays: transform, filter, and calculate
A small project: calculate an order total

assignment.title: Build and explain your order calculator
assignment.instructions:
Submit JavaScript code for orderTotal(items) and a short explanation. Use integer cents. Include at least four checks: empty order, multiple items, zero quantity, and invalid quantity. Explain your validation and an overflow case. Paste your code and reasoning into the answer field.

Assessment / 100: correct totals 40; validation 25; meaningful checks 25; clear explanation 10. The teacher reviews and grades the submission.

title: SQL foundations for application developers
description: Design small relational tables, read data with joins, and protect related writes with a transaction. Text-based technical course with a practical schema/query assignment. Graduation demonstration course.

lessons.title: Tables, keys, and relationships
lessons.content:
A primary key identifies one row. A foreign key links a row to a related table. A unique constraint prevents duplicate values or pairs.

```sql
CREATE TABLE students (
  id TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
  name TEXT NOT NULL
);
CREATE TABLE enrollments (
  student_id TEXT NOT NULL REFERENCES students(id),
  course_id TEXT NOT NULL,
  UNIQUE(student_id, course_id)
);
```

In a complete schema, course_id should also reference a courses table. With SQLite, enable PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON for each connection before relying on foreign-key enforcement.

Practice: describe the error a duplicate student/course pair should produce and why application validation alone is insufficient.

lessons.title: SELECT, filtering, and joins
lessons.content:
```sql
SELECT chooses columns; WHERE limits rows; JOIN relates matching records.
```

```sql
SELECT s.name, e.course_id
FROM students AS s
JOIN enrollments AS e ON e.student_id = s.id
WHERE e.course_id = ?
ORDER BY s.name;
```

Bind the course ID as a parameter rather than concatenating untrusted input. An INNER JOIN excludes students without a matching enrollment. A LEFT JOIN can keep them and return NULL for missing enrollment fields.

To count enrollments per student, group by the student key and count a non-null enrollment column. COUNT(*) with a LEFT JOIN would also count the placeholder row for a student with no enrollments.

Practice: write a query listing every student and their enrollment count, including zero.

lessons.title: Transactions and reliable changes
lessons.content:
A transaction groups related changes so they commit together or roll back together.

```sql
BEGIN;
-- Insert an order header.
-- Insert each order line.
COMMIT;
```

If a required line insert fails, roll back the transaction instead of leaving an incomplete order. Do not catch and ignore errors inside a transaction.

Keep transactions short and avoid network calls while holding database locks. Choose indexes based on real query patterns; an index improves some reads but also adds write and storage cost.

Practice: explain where you would start, commit, and roll back a transaction when enrolling one student in two required modules as a single operation.

assignment.title: Model a small learning catalog
assignment.instructions:
Submit CREATE TABLE statements for students, courses, and enrollments with appropriate primary/foreign keys and a unique student/course pair. Add a parameterized query listing students in one course and a query returning enrollment counts including zero. Explain one transaction you would use.

Assessment / 100: schema 40; queries 40; transaction explanation 20.

title: HTTP and APIs: a practical first workflow
description: Follow a browser request through an API, understand status codes and validation, and design a complete enrollment interaction. Text-based technical course. Graduation demonstration course.

lessons.title: Requests and responses
lessons.content:
An HTTP request has a method, a target, headers, and sometimes a body. The response has a status, headers, and sometimes a body.

```http
POST /api/courses/example/enroll
Authorization: Bearer <token>
Content-Type: application/json
```

The server must derive the current account from verified authentication, not from an arbitrary user_id in the request body.

A successful enrollment can return 201 Created with a new enrollment identifier. A duplicate can return 409 Conflict. A missing or invalid session receives 401; an authenticated account without permission receives 403.

Practice: describe which component makes the final permission decision, even when the interface hides an unavailable action.

lessons.title: Handle loading, success, and failure
Validate on the server and verify the workflow
lessons.content:
Client-side validation is useful feedback. Server-side validation enforces the contract. Database constraints preserve essential invariants.

For an enrollment endpoint, verify:
1. No session is rejected.
2. A teacher cannot enroll as a student.
3. A draft course is unavailable to a new student.
4. A valid student can enroll in a published course.
5. A repeated request does not create another enrollment.

Also verify the returned account cannot read another student's private notes or submission. Include failures in your evidence instead of recording only successful calls.

Practice: create a small expected/actual/status table for those checks and describe the starting database state.

assignment.title: Design a reliable enrollment endpoint
assignment.instructions:
Describe the request, authentication, authorization, validation, database operation, successful response, and error cases for enrollment. Add five meaningful verification cases with expected statuses. Explain how the interface handles a failed request without inventing a successful enrollment.

Assessment / 100: end-to-end flow 40; permission/error handling 30; verification cases 30.
